clue.text: Early gift for Peter and Gertrude

explanation.surface: A first present handed to a couple called Peter and Gertrude.
explanation.walkthrough: A hansel (or handsel) is a gift for good luck at a beginning, such as a new year. In Humperdinck's opera Hansel and Gretel the children's parents are Peter and Gertrude, so 'for Peter and Gertrude' points to their son.
explanation.definitionFit: The first sense is an old word for a good-luck present at a start; the second is the boy whose parents bear those names in Humperdinck's opera.

clue.text: Fondness shown by "Marguerite Duras" for John Hersey work

definitions.text: shown by "Marguerite Duras" for John Hersey work

explanation.surface: Affection that a French writer displays towards an American reporter's book.
explanation.walkthrough: John Hersey's book is Hiroshima; Marguerite Duras wrote the screenplay Hiroshima mon amour, so the French word she adds after that title is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Fondness is love, French amour; and amour is the last word Duras tacks on to Hersey's title Hiroshima.

clue.text: Stubborn defender of duodecimal system?

parts.note: a 'duodecimal system' reads like counting in twelves, but here it is the twelve-tone method of composition, and its stubborn champion is the Viennese composer who invented it

explanation.surface: A diehard who argues for counting in twelves instead of tens.
explanation.definitionFit: The Austrian composer devised twelve-tone serialism and defended it doggedly against critics.

clue.text: Imperial survivor of Shakespearean bloodbath

parts.note: Titus Andronicus is Shakespeare's bloodiest play; Titus's son outlives the slaughter and is hailed as Rome's new emperor at the end

explanation.surface: A ruler who lived through one of Shakespeare's massacres.
explanation.definitionFit: Titus's surviving son becomes emperor of Rome in the final scene of Titus Andronicus.

clue.text: Spotted trend in abstract painting

parts.note: 'spotted' seems to mean noticed, but the movement is named from the French for a spot or blot, being painting in dabs of colour

explanation.surface: Someone notices a new fashion among abstract painters.
explanation.definitionFit: The French style of abstract painting in blots and dabs of colour takes its name from tache, a spot.

clue.text: Van Gogh subjects in Chips with Everything?

definitions.text: Van Gogh subjects in Chips with Everything?

parts.words: Van Gogh subjects in Chips with Everything?
parts.note: Chips with Everything is Arnold Wesker's play, but read literally it is a diet of fried potatoes, the food of the peasants in Van Gogh's dark 1885 painting

explanation.surface: Van Gogh's sitters appearing in Wesker's play about national service.
explanation.walkthrough: Chips with Everything is a 1962 play by Arnold Wesker; British 'chips' are fried potato sticks (American fries).
explanation.definitionFit: Van Gogh's famous painting shows a peasant family at supper on potatoes, people who would eat chips with everything.

clue.text: He perceived the way of the world

definitions.text: He perceived the way of the world

parts.words: He perceived the way of the world
parts.note: it reads as praise of a worldly-wise man, but The Way of the World is a 1700 comedy, so this is its playwright

explanation.surface: A tribute to a shrewd observer of how life works.
explanation.definitionFit: William Congreve wrote the Restoration comedy The Way of the World, satirising fashionable society.

clue.text: Pseudonym of gaudy author

parts.note: 'gaudy' seems to mean flashy, but The Gaudy is a novel by J. I. M. Stewart, who wrote detective stories under a pen name

explanation.surface: The pen name used by a flamboyant writer.
explanation.walkthrough: A gaudy is an Oxford college reunion feast; Stewart's novel The Gaudy is named after one.
explanation.definitionFit: J. I. M. Stewart, author of The Gaudy, published his Appleby mysteries as Michael Innes.

clue.text: Remind wit about Buchan work

indicators.note: 'about' here means turned around and scattered, so the letters of these two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: An instruction to jog a joker's memory about a Scottish novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' asks for the ten letters of REMIND and WIT to be rearranged. John Buchan's 1923 novel shares its name with the depth of winter.
explanation.definitionFit: Midwinter is a 1923 historical novel by John Buchan, author of The Thirty-Nine Steps.

clue.text: Dramatist's style makes Pooh's mess spotless

indicators.note: a mess is a muddle, so the letters of the bear's name with its possessive are jumbled

explanation.surface: A tidied-up bear's muddle shows the manner of a Greek tragedian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pooh's' is the bear's name with its possessive, so all five letters, S included, go into the anagram that 'mess' signals; Sophoclean describes the manner of Sophocles.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes the manner of Sophocles, the Athenian tragedian who wrote Oedipus Rex.

clue.text: Unadorned theme of Kenneth Clark

explanation.surface: A plain subject for an art historian.
explanation.walkthrough: Kenneth Clark's 1956 study is The Nude: A Study in Ideal Form.
explanation.definitionFit: Unadorned means bare or unclothed; and the undressed human figure was the subject of Kenneth Clark's book.

clue.text: "If any be —'s legs, these are they: thou art very — indeed" (The Tempest)

definitions.text: "If any be —'s legs, these are they: thou art very — indeed" (The Tempest)

parts.words: "If any be —'s legs, these are they: thou art very — indeed" (The Tempest)
parts.note: the quotation is Stephano finding his drunken friend under Caliban's cloak; the blanks are that friend's name, the jester in The Tempest

explanation.surface: A line from The Tempest with a character's name blanked out.
explanation.definitionFit: The jester in The Tempest is pulled by his legs from under Caliban's gaberdine by Stephano, who speaks this line.

clue.text: Critic takes ski run apart

indicators.note: 'apart' means taken to pieces, so the letters of ski and run are broken up and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A reviewer pulls apart a ski slope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'apart' rearranges the six letters of SKI and RUN.
explanation.definitionFit: John Ruskin was the leading Victorian art critic, author of Modern Painters.

clue.text: French writer's vocation lost in Arab bedsit

indicators.note: 'lost in' says the word is buried inside the run of these two words

explanation.surface: A French author's calling vanishes in a cheap room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lost in' hides the word across 'arAB BEdsit'. Several French writers, such as the Abbé Prévost, were priests by calling.
explanation.definitionFit: An abbé is a French cleric, the calling of writers like the Abbé Prévost of Manon Lescaut.

clue.text: Something Beastly for Durrell's psychiatrist?

parts.note: Balthazar is the doctor in Durrell's Alexandria Quartet; Donleavy's novel The Beastly ... of Balthazar B gives the single blessing this asks for

explanation.surface: Something horrible awaits a psychiatrist in a Durrell novel.
explanation.definitionFit: A beatitude is a blessing; J. P. Donleavy's novel title pairs the plural with 'Beastly' and the name Balthazar, also a Durrell title.

clue.text: Recommend lawyer from West

explanation.surface: A request to suggest a solicitor from the western side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'West' is the novelist Morris West, whose book is The Devil's Advocate.
explanation.definitionFit: To recommend is to speak in favour of; and the counsel in Morris West's novel The Devil's Advocate argues against canonisation.

clue.text: Bardic gem produced by university

indicators.note: 'produced' means made into something new, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A poetic jewel is the work of a university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'produced' rearranges the nine letters of BARDIC and GEM.
explanation.definitionFit: Cambridge is one of England's two ancient universities.

clue.text: Novelist seen to cavort with model in scam

indicators.note: 'in' places the cavorting and the model inside the word for a scam

parts.note: a con is a swindle or scam
to romp is to play about boisterously, to cavort
the Model T was Ford's famous car, so 'model' gives T

explanation.surface: A writer is seen frolicking with a model during a swindle.
explanation.walkthrough: Richmal Crompton wrote the Just William books.
explanation.definitionFit: Richmal Crompton was the English writer of the Just William stories for children.

clue.text: Milne characters brought together by D. H. Lawrence

indicators.note: 'brought together' joins the two names side by side into one word

parts.note: Kanga is the mother ... in A. A. Milne's Winnie-the-Pooh
Roo is Kanga's baby in the same Milne stories

explanation.surface: A. A. Milne's animals are united by a modernist novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a metonym: 'D. H. Lawrence' stands for a book by him, his 1923 Australian novel Kangaroo.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawrence's 1923 novel, set in Australia, bears the name of the marsupial.

clue.text: Some further work of Max Beerbohm

explanation.surface: A request for another piece by an Edwardian essayist.
explanation.walkthrough: Max Beerbohm published essay collections titled The Works of Max Beerbohm and then More (1899).
explanation.definitionFit: Further means additional or extra; and Beerbohm's second book of essays was called More, following his Works.

clue.text: Sweetly inspirational poet associated with Sullivan operetta

definitions.text: Sweetly inspirational poet associated with Sullivan operetta

parts.words: Sweetly inspirational poet associated with Sullivan operetta
parts.note: the clue describes a poet by surname, L. A. G. ..., through a link with one of Arthur Sullivan's light operas

explanation.surface: A poet of gentle uplift connected with a light opera by Sullivan.
explanation.definitionFit: L. A. G. Strong was an English poet and novelist of the twentieth century.

clue.text: "I'm Irma": misleading statement by femme fatale in Hawthorne story

indicators.note: a misleading statement is twisted, so the letters of the quoted words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A seductress lies about her name in a Hawthorne tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'misleading' rearranges the letters of I'M IRMA.
explanation.definitionFit: Miriam is the dark, mysterious painter at the centre of Hawthorne's novel The Marble Faun.

clue.text: Brand loyalty is expected of his admirers

definitions.text: Brand loyalty is expected of his admirers

parts.words: Brand loyalty is expected of his admirers
parts.note: 'Brand loyalty' sounds like marketing, but Brand is an 1865 verse drama by a Norwegian playwright, whose fans would stand by it

explanation.surface: A marketing remark that fans should stay faithful to a product.
explanation.definitionFit: Henrik Ibsen wrote the verse play Brand, about an uncompromising priest.

clue.text: Fertility goddess seen in a store that's inexhaustible

indicators.note: 'seen in' says the goddess can be found inside the run of these words

explanation.surface: A goddess of fertility appears in a shop with endless stock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seen in' hides the name at the start of 'A STORE THat's'; 'inexhaustible' only dresses the store in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Ashtoreth is the Hebrew Bible's name for the Phoenician fertility goddess Astarte.

clue.text: Northernmost destination of Longfellow

parts.note: Longfellow's late collection is Ultima ..., named after the ancients' furthest land to the north

explanation.surface: The poet's journey ending at the most northerly place.
explanation.definitionFit: Ultima Thule was the classical name for the farthest northern land, and Longfellow used it as a book title.

clue.text: Sprouts affectionately referred to by Bates

explanation.surface: Young shoots mentioned fondly by a novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: H. E. Bates wrote The Darling Buds of May, taking the phrase from Shakespeare's eighteenth sonnet.
explanation.definitionFit: Sprouts are new shoots on a plant; and Bates's title calls them 'darling', an affectionate term.

clue.text: Poe creature which may have bitten some B. Traven protagonists

definitions.text: which may have bitten some B. Traven protagonists

explanation.surface: An insect from Poe that might have nipped the heroes of a Traven novel.
explanation.walkthrough: In B. Traven's The Treasure of the Sierra Madre the prospectors are consumed by greed; 'bitten by the gold bug' means seized by gold fever.
explanation.definitionFit: Poe's story centres on a golden beetle; and the same phrase names the lust for gold that grips Traven's prospectors.

clue.text: He went to school at Linbury Court in 1950

definitions.text: He went to school at Linbury Court in 1950

parts.words: He went to school at Linbury Court in 1950
parts.note: Linbury Court is the prep school in Anthony Buckeridge's stories, and the first book of 1950 sends its hero there

explanation.surface: A biographical note about a boy's schooling.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Buckeridge's schoolboy hero first appeared in book form in Jennings Goes to School, 1950.

clue.text: Reportedly grim sibling of!

parts.note: 'Reportedly grim' sounds like the Brothers Grimm, who collected the folk tale; 1 across names her brother

explanation.surface: A bleak relative of an earlier entry.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Grimms' fairy tale the girl lost in the woods is Hansel's sister.
